title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open-source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
content:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open-source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025.
“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X.
The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open-source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance.
As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open-source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space.
After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October. While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models.
The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Collette Kress were not returned.
Huang’s advocacy for open-source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X. The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.”
Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated.
In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs.
Earlier this year, Huang promoted open-source AI during his January keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, noting that open-source models have “really revolutionized artificial intelligence.

report.summary: Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue calls Jensen Huang's exit a 'sad day' and vows to keep fighting for open-source AI as Nvidia's $12.9B acquisition proceeds.
report.background: In September, Nvidia announced plans to buy Hugging Face — the main hub for open-source AI models — for $12.9 billion, the company's second-largest deal after its $20 billion purchase of chipmaker Groq's assets in December 2025. Jensen Huang had been one of the tech industry's most vocal advocates for open-weight AI: he signed a July policy letter with 25 companies urging Washington not to over-restrict downloadable models, pushed a $6 billion partnership with coding startup Poolside, and expanded the open Nemotron model family. That record made his departure as CEO a symbolic blow. The deal is also under scrutiny — the U.S. Department of Justice began asking in October how it would affect competition — and it is still slated to close in the first half of 2027, leaving open-source advocates uncertain about Nvidia's posture in the interim.
key_points: Huang was open source's most powerful ally: he signed a 25-company letter defending open-weight models, funded Poolside's open ecosystem, and shipped Nemotron models. His exit removes a prominent champion from inside the world's most valuable AI chipmaker, which is why Delangue framed the news as a 'really sad day.'

The $12.9 billion Hugging Face acquisition is still moving forward, with closing targeted for the first half of 2027. Nvidia pledged to preserve open support, but owning the main distribution channel for AI models would give it unusual influence over which models get discovered, hosted and promoted.

Regulators are watching. The Justice Department's inquiries into competitive effects add a second layer of uncertainty on top of leadership turmoil, and neither Nvidia nor Hugging Face has clarified how the deal or its open-source commitments might change under interim CEO Collette Kress.

Delangue used the moment to reassure the community rather than retreat, writing on X that Hugging Face will keep fighting for open-source AI 'harder than ever' because the issue is 'too important to slow down now' — positioning the platform as an independent advocate even as it is being absorbed.

Open-weight momentum is now global and competitive. Huang's argument was that open models expand access, strengthen competition and prevent vendor lock-in, and Nvidia's own roadmap — a 120-billion-parameter Nemotron for enterprise agents plus lightweight Bolt models for PCs — shows the strategy predates any single leader.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the signal matters more than the org chart: if Nvidia softens its open-weight advocacy, the main counterweight to closed, API-only frontier labs weakens, and policy debates in Washington could tilt toward restriction. Developers face practical uncertainty — Hugging Face's hosting, licensing and model-distribution terms are the backbone of countless workflows, and any shift toward Nvidia-favored models or hardware would ripple through tooling. Regular users are affected indirectly but broadly: open-weight models are what make local, private, low-cost AI possible on laptops and on-premise servers, and they underpin price competition against proprietary APIs. Delangue's vow offers reassurance, but the real test is whether Nvidia, under new leadership and antitrust pressure, keeps funding open ecosystems at the same pace — or treats Hugging Face primarily as a distribution channel for its own silicon.
report.tools: Watch the Hugging Face Hub itself for model releases, licensing changes and community governance signals. Nvidia's Nemotron family (including the 120B agent model and lightweight Bolt variants) is the clearest test of its open-weight commitment. For running open models locally, try Ollama or LM Studio; for production serving, vLLM and SGLang. Keep an eye on Poolside's open coding ecosystem and on open-weight policy trackers following the 25-company letter, since regulatory filings often reveal deal terms before announcements do.
